https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: CHARLOTTESVILLE—Twenty years ago, I argued that the creation of databases of sensitive information—including home addresses, biometric data, and Social Security numbers—should be understood as ultrahazardous activities. They could be managed only if the entities creating them were held fully liable for breaches. As AI models generate new and extreme risks, the need for a strict-liability regime is urgent. If frontier companies bore strict responsibility for the destruction caused by their AI chatbots and agents, they might slow down to figure out how to conduct their activities safely and change course where that is not possible.
LONDON—Two recent conversations confirmed my suspicion that too many experts are operating in silos and often failing to connect the dots.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: SÃO PAULO/BUENOS AIRES—Brazil’s presidential election is headed to a runoff. Flávio Bolsonaro—son of disgraced former President Jair Bolsonaro—finished ahead of the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the first round, but neither gained the majority needed to win outright.

BERLIN—During his recent visit to Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced that China would send a breeding pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The “envoys of friendship,” Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived just a few days later. This is hardly the first time China has used its iconic bear as an instrument of soft power. By loaning the animals to overseas zoos, it seeks to project an image of China not as a threatening dragon, but rather as a tough but cuddly charmer.

CHICAGO—For most of the past four decades, China’s direction of travel was clear: everything was moving forward. The country’s per capita GDP was barely $300 at the start of the 1990s. But its cities would soon fill with skyscrapers, highways, and subways. Families that once worried about having enough food would buy apartments, cars, and smartphones. Children would go to universities their parents could scarcely have imagined attending. In the space of a generation, China joined the World Trade Organization, hosted the Olympics, built the world’s largest high-speed rail network, and became a central engine of the global economy.

BEIJING—The renminbi is back at the center of debates about global macroeconomic imbalances. With China’s merchandise trade surplus widening to $1.2 trillion in 2025, and with its manufacturing sector becoming increasingly dominant, the near-consensus among financial and economic commentators is that the renminbi is significantly undervalued. The implication is that China should let its currency appreciate sharply, thereby shrinking its surplus, easing competitive pressure on manufacturers elsewhere, and helping rebalance the global economy.

LONDON—Whether a hospital can hire nurses, a school can repair its roof, or a country can build a clean-energy grid often depends on factors that rarely make the news. For many governments, rules limiting deficits, debt, or spending ultimately determine whether they can invest in the future.

BERLIN—Recent state elections in Germany have been portrayed as momentous, since the far right finished first in two and may well come to power in one. Yet future historians may focus on another, largely overlooked outcome: For the first time in the post-World War II period, Germany’s Christian Democrats (CDU) failed to pass the 5% electoral threshold. Worse, this disastrous result occurred in the largely rural state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where former Chancellor Angela Merkel chaired the CDU’s state branch for close to seven years.

YOGYAKARTA—Interdependence may be the theme of this year’s annual meeting of the Intergovernmental Forum on Mining, Minerals, Metals, and Sustainable Development (IGF), held in Geneva on October 12–14, but competition between countries to secure transition minerals remains intense. This scramble could have dire consequences for mineral-producing countries if it undermines sustainability standards and prevents equitable cost- and benefit-sharing between and within countries.

The International Energy Agency estimates that, to achieve net-zero emissions, demand for critical minerals will triple by 2030 and quadruple by 2040. Mineral-rich countries, aware of the “resource curse,” are seeking ways to retain control over their reserves. In a bid to promote domestic value addition and meet their economic-development objectives, many of these countries are pursuing export bans on critical raw materials.

But Indonesia’s experience as one of the first countries to implement such a ban shows that downstream industrialization is not a cure-all. It can come with substantial environmental and social costs, and the benefits are not always shared equitably with the local communities that often bear the greatest burden of extraction and processing. And while extraction, smelting, and processing have boosted economic growth in Indonesia’s three nickel-rich provinces, they have not contributed significantly to the national economy. Frontier-making—the act of transforming marginal areas into centers of resource extraction—can create new “sacrifice zones” when not accompanied by robust regulation and democratic oversight.

Meanwhile, the emphasis on sustainable mining has never been greater at the global level. In 2024, the United Nations Secretary-General’s Panel on Critical Energy Transition Minerals released a set of guiding principles that underscore the need for a new paradigm rooted in justice and equity, and for mining to benefit host countries and local communities. Regional frameworks, including the African Union’s Africa Mining Vision, its follow-up guidelines and frameworks, and the ASEAN Principles for Sustainable Minerals Development, reflect similar commitments.

These agreements are sidelined, however, when countries pursue bilateral agreements that prioritize market access over all else. Consider the uneven treatment of nickel and palm oil in the EU–Indonesia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. The European Union has strict sustainability standards for palm oil, but not for nickel, even though both sectors can cause significant social and environmental degradation.

The best way to put principles into practice is to consolidate Global South policy and advocacy networks. This would enable policymakers, civil society, and local communities to share their experience with mineral extraction and processing and their proposals for making the sector more equitable and environmentally responsible.

There is a genuine desire among policymakers in the Global South to share the lessons learned from their successes and failures. The Natural Resource Governance Institute’s South–South Transition Minerals Learning Platform has facilitated the dissemination of policy insights among government officials from Indonesia, Chile, Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and other countries. While they share the same goal—to build more inclusive, resilient, and prosperous societies using mineral wealth—the platform enables a deeper understanding of how variations in commodities, domestic political economies, and value-chain positions require different strategies, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

Equally important are transnational or transcalar advocacy networks that connect civil-society groups across the Global South. They, too, can provide a platform for sharing experience and knowledge, while also strengthening collective action and extending accountability beyond national borders. By producing wide-ranging evidence of social and environmental abuses linked to mineral extraction, smelting, and processing, domestic advocacy actors can bypass governments and companies that do not adequately support local communities and directly seek out international allies to apply outside pressure.

Here, again, Indonesia provides a useful example. The prominent Indonesian NGO WALHI, together with Friends of the Earth Japan, mobilized more than one hundred organizations to urge Vale Indonesia’s shareholders to act on alleged human-rights abuses at the Sorowako nickel project. Some shareholders, including Vale, Sumitomo Metal Mining, and Mitsui & Co., responded by exerting pressure on the company when the government failed to do so effectively.

Similarly, campaigners from Mighty Earth, Climate Rights International, and Global Witness attracted investors’ attention by alleging widespread abuses in Indonesia’s nickel extraction and processing industry. They urged electric-vehicle battery and car producers to comply with social and environmental standards and due-diligence obligations. Weda Bay Nickel has since expressed interest in complying with Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance standards, and some automakers have imposed stricter requirements on nickel suppliers.

This global pressure—which includes Publish What You Pay Indonesia raising concerns about the country’s nickel governance at the 2025 OECD Forum on Responsible Mineral Supply Chains—has forced the Indonesian government’s hand. After assessing the gap between its regulatory framework and three global standards, the government is preparing ESG (environmental, social, and governance) guidelines to help firms identify which Indonesian regulations meet the requirements of global standards in the nickel supply chain.

Advancing inclusion in transition-mineral supply chains—the goal of the IGF meeting—requires strategies for translating lofty declarations into concrete action. This can be achieved by bringing together and strengthening Global South policy and advocacy networks. Existing South–South cooperation mechanisms can expand their reach to facilitate policy learning on critical minerals, while domestic civil-society groups can deepen their global connections to put a spotlight on mining-related environmental destruction and human-rights abuses. Many pieces of the puzzle are already in place; now it is time to put them together.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: PARIS—Jordan Bardella is little known outside of France. But if Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally (RN), wins next spring’s presidential election—as appears increasingly likely—he will, she says, be her prime minister. The question is whether the growing scandal around Bardella will cause Le Pen to change her mind and, if not, how that will affect her chances of victory.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.byline: Angela Huyue Zhang and Yue Zhao
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: LOS ANGELES—Hardly a week goes by without another report of an AI agent from a leading US lab digitally breaching businesses or even government services. In July, OpenAI agents escaped an internal testing environment and attacked the collaboration-platform company Hugging Face. In June, another OpenAI model gained nonpublic access to an Australian government Medicare statistics service while trying to complete a research task. And in the latest revelation, an Anthropic agent broke into the US State Department website and filled out visa applications.

JAIPUR—It is difficult to remember a time when economies, financial markets, politics, and societies were subject to significant volatility and uncertainty simultaneously, let alone to the degree they are today.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.byline: Barry Eichengreen, Will Fithian and Wesley Holliday
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: BERKELEY—Dario Amodei, a co-founder of Anthropic, among others, has warned that AI poses an existential threat to humankind. Others have gone further and argued for pausing the training of new frontier AI models. The counterargument is that regulation, including self-regulation, is unlikely to be effective. And even if a pause is feasible in principle, there is little hope that it could be sustained in practice, given that the United States and China desperately fear falling behind each other.

TORONTO—Attacks on one’s reputation used to be the price that celebrities paid for fame. But now it is a hazard of ordinary life. Anyone with any standing to lose is vulnerable. If you have an online presence, the damage can spread much further and faster than the truth. Run-of-the-mill bad publicity or harassment might dent your confidence or cause annoyance, but if you become the target of a technologically augmented campaign aimed at destroying your reputation, you could lose much more.

SÃO PAULO/STIRLING—The enormous climate, water, and biodiversity benefits generated by tropical forests accrue to the entire world. But hardly any of the economic value created is captured by the countries and communities that safeguard them. The Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) was launched at last year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Belém to start correcting this imbalance.

For too long, it has been more profitable to destroy tropical forests than to conserve them, even though they provide services essential for the survival of many countries and for the welfare of us all. The Amazon recycles nearly half of its rainfall and exports moisture that shapes precipitation patterns across South America and beyond. The Congo Basin, with its peatlands that store roughly 30 billion tons of carbon, is one of the planet’s great carbon reservoirs, while many of the plant and animal species in Borneo are found nowhere else on Earth.

Moreover, across the tropics, forests support the livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people—including Indigenous communities whose stewardship is often essential for maintaining them—while also sustaining local cultures and bolstering food and water security.

But market prices do not adequately reflect these benefits, creating an economic barrier that all tropical regions bump up against: in the short term, clearing a hectare of forest can generate more income than protecting it, even when the long-term costs of forest loss are much greater. As a result, cattle ranching and agricultural expansion exert enormous pressure on the Amazon, small- and large-scale agriculture contribute to forest conversion in the Congo Basin, and industrial plantations have transformed sylvan landscapes in Southeast Asia.

Worryingly, a recent brief by the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network emphasizes that international public finance remains far below the estimated investment required for conserving tropical forests, and that competition for declining official development aid is intensifying.

Grants and concessional loans remain indispensable for strengthening institutions, protecting rights, restoring degraded landscapes, and supporting activities with large social and ecological returns but limited commercial returns. Yet, traditional development finance alone cannot close the gap. Nor should scarce public resources be used simply to absorb risks for private investors.

This is where the TFFF comes in. It is designed to provide eligible tropical-forest countries with predictable, long-term payments for maintaining forest cover and meeting agreed performance criteria. This changes the economic incentives: according to the TFFF’s current model, countries will forgo around $400 per deforested hectare. Because each hectare of standing tropical forest increases a country’s payment, policymakers may be more willing to implement robust national strategies that complement the TFFF, like Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD+).

The TFFF’s proposed architecture includes a commitment to direct at least 20% of payments to Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities, who play an outsize role in protecting forests but have historically received only a small share of international climate and nature finance. The real test will be whether this commitment results in predictable funding that reaches those managing forests on the ground and, in the process, reinforces local governance.

Of course, the TFFF is not a silver bullet. No single solution can close the financing gap for tropical-forest conservation. Public and private funding, domestic expenditure, concessional loans, grants, results-based payments, and new investment mechanisms must all play a role. Perhaps more importantly, no financial mechanism can compensate indefinitely for incentives that continue to encourage deforestation. To change them, policymakers must intervene.

The TFFF has a role to play here, too. To succeed, it must not only mobilize enough capital to translate global commitments into predictable payments on the ground, but also support governments in implementing policies that protect forests and complement existing forest-finance instruments. These include strengthening land rights and environmental governance, repurposing harmful subsidies, supporting restoration, and expanding viable economic opportunities compatible with standing forests.

For decades, the international community has acknowledged the extraordinary value of tropical forests while failing to invest adequately in their conservation. Ensuring that they remain standing is in everyone’s interests. The challenge now is to use all tools at our disposal, not least the TFFF, to turn talk into action.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: TORONTO—Earlier this year, when I first described the guiding principle of Donald Trump’s foreign policy as superpower suicide, it was already obvious that the US President’s war of whimsy against Iran was a strategic catastrophe. Five months on, this failure is all the more glaring. Worse, it has provided Trump with another pretext to reward Russia. Weakness has begotten more weakness.

MELBOURNE—“Americanism, not effective altruism.” That’s a new slogan launched on X by the US Department of “War,” the words running across an image of President Donald Trump saluting. Above the image, the post reads: “The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!”

NEW YORK—On September 25, a Moscow court sent the political analyst Alexander Kynev to pretrial detention for “large-scale illegal drug production, sale, and trafficking”—a charge that could land him in prison for 10–20 years. But no evidence of Kynev’s involvement in illegal drugs has been made public.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/onpoin.body: OXFORD—The divide between AI fantasists and doomsters is growing. The fantasists believe AI will turbocharge growth and create a utopian world of abundance. The doomsters believe it poses an existential threat to humanity and that, before killing us, it will lead to mass unemployment and a world of pervasive surveillance and alternative realities. Who is right? And can governments do anything to mitigate the risk of catastrophe?

WASHINGTON, DC—China’s surveillance state reaches into the most banal corners of life. At a garden in Yangzhou, visitors must scan their faces to receive toilet paper; the dispenser remembers them and refuses to provide a second serving. In Shenzhen, the police use facial-recognition technology to catch jaywalkers, then send penalties to scofflaws’ phones and notify their employers. The scrutiny is not limited to public spaces. For China-registered users, WeChat messages and images are automatically screened. One human-rights lawyer recalled that police monitored his WeChat exchanges before detaining and torturing him.
